summary: This packet decomposes the rational-points programme from six primary sources. Two come from the supplied library: Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves (2nd ed., VIII.1-VIII.6, VIII.9, IX.1-IX.4, X.1, X.4), and Faltings 1983 (Lemma 4 and Satz 7). Four are authorized public copies fetched for this job: Poonen, Rational points on varieties (Sections 5.7, 6.5.7, Chapter 8, Section 9.5); Zhang, Equidistribution of small points on abelian varieties (Annals 1998); Ullmo, Positivite et discretion des points algebriques des courbes (arXiv alg-geom/9606017); and Szpiro-Ullmo-Zhang, Equirepartition des petits points (Invent. Math. 1997). RP.0 covers heights on projective space, Northcott, heights on elliptic curves and the Neron-Tate height (elliptic case only). RP.1 covers the Kummer-theory weak Mordell-Weil theorem, the descent theorem, Mordell-Weil for elliptic curves, positive definiteness of the height pairing, torsor evaluation, finiteness of H^1_S and of Selmer sets, weak Mordell-Weil for abelian varieties, Selmer/Sha sequences, and two worked 2-descents (y^2 = x^3 - 12x^2 + 20x, y^2 = x^3 - 6x^2 + 17x). RP.2 covers F-obstruction sets, the Brauer-Manin pairing and reciprocity, local constancy, Iskovskikh's obstructed surface and a quadric bundle with nonempty Brauer set but no rational points. RP.3 covers descent sets, Minchev, Br = PGL-descent, etale-Brauer = descent (sketch), Cao's iteration theorem and insufficiency of all these obstructions. RP.4 covers the Parshin reduction with uniform field control, Siegel for elliptic and genus-one curves via Roth, and the S-unit route. RP.5 covers equidistribution, Zhang's Bogomolov theorem and Ullmo's curve case. RP.6 records the frontier register, the function-field analogue, Jacobian points and worked examples. Corrections found in the sources: Silverman Proposition VIII.5.4(c) (exponent), Example X.4.5.1 (the 2-Selmer group is (Z/2Z)^3, not (Z/2Z)^2) and Proposition X.4.9 (a^2 - 4b, not a^2 - b). All stages remain partial: the general height machine, Mordell-Lang, Roth and Siegel in general, the Brauer-group chapters, Arakelov intersection theory and the cited comparison theorems are unread imports.

nodes.title: The height H_K on P^N(K), its independence of coordinates, its behaviour under field extension, and the absolute height
nodes.statement: For a number field K with the standard absolute values M_K and local degrees n_v = [K_v : Q_v], and P = [x_0, ..., x_N] in P^N(K), define H_K(P) = prod_{v in M_K} max{|x_0|_v, ..., |x_N|_v}^{n_v}. Then (a) H_K(P) does not depend on the homogeneous coordinates, (b) H_K(P) >= 1, and (c) for a finite extension L/K, H_L(P) = H_K(P)^{[L:K]}. The absolute height H(P) = H_K(P)^{1/[K:Q]}, for any number field K with P in P^N(K), is well defined on P^N(Qbar) and satisfies H(P) >= 1; the logarithmic height is h(P) = log H(P) >= 0. For K = Q and coprime integer coordinates, H_Q(P) = max |x_i|. Galois conjugation preserves H: H(P^sigma) = H(P) for sigma in Gal(Qbar/Q).
hypotheses: M_Q consists of the usual absolute value and the p-adic absolute values normalized by |p^n a/b|_p = p^{-n} for p not dividing ab; M_K is the set of absolute values of K restricting to one of these

Imported without proof (Silverman: "see any standard text on algebraic number theory"): the extension formula sum_{w | v} n_w = [L:K] n_v (5.2) and the product formula prod_v |x|_v^{n_v} = 1 for x in K^* (5.3); these belong to the number-field supplier (FoundationsAndLibraryIntegration LI.4)

Correction: the printed statement of Proposition 5.4(c) reads H_L(P) = H_K(P)^{1/[K:Q]}; the printed proof on the same page ends with H_L(P) = H_K(P)^{[L:K]}, which is the correct statement and the one used to define the absolute height
proofSteps: (a) Replacing (x_i) by (lambda x_i) multiplies the product by prod_v |lambda|_v^{n_v} = 1 (product formula).
(b) Choose coordinates with some x_j = 1; then every local factor is at least 1.
(c) For x_i in K, max_i |x_i|_w = max_i |x_i|_v for w | v, so the product over w | v of the local factors is the v-factor raised to sum_{w|v} n_w = [L:K] n_v (extension formula).
Absolute height: by (c) the [K:Q]-th root does not depend on K; by (b) it is at least 1.
K = Q (Remark 5.5): with coprime integer coordinates every p-adic factor equals 1, so only the archimedean factor max |x_i| remains.
Galois invariance (Theorem 5.10): sigma identifies M_K with M_{K^sigma} with |x^sigma|_{v^sigma} = |x|_v and n_v = n_{v^sigma}, so H_{K^sigma}(P^sigma) = H_K(P) and [K^sigma : Q] = [K : Q].
acceptance: Test independence of projective coordinates on a point of P^2(Q(i)) by scaling with a non-unit, and independence of the field by computing H_K and H_L for L = K(sqrt 2).
Check the corrected exponent [L:K] against the proof, not the printed statement 1/[K:Q].
Check that the normalization of M_K (not the normalized valuations ord_v) is the one for which the product formula holds with exponents n_v.

nodes.title: Theorem VIII.5.6: a degree-d morphism of projective spaces multiplies heights by H^d up to constants
nodes.statement: Let F : P^N -> P^M be a morphism of degree d, given by homogeneous polynomials f_0, ..., f_M over Qbar of degree d with no common zero other than 0. There are positive constants C_1, C_2 depending on F such that C_1 H(P)^d <= H(F(P)) <= C_2 H(P)^d for all P in P^N(Qbar). In particular (Corollary 5.8) an automorphism of P^N given by A in GL_{N+1}(Qbar) changes H by bounded factors.
hypotheses: The upper bound holds without the hypothesis that the f_j have no common nontrivial zero; the lower bound needs it (Exercise 8.10 gives counterexamples otherwise)
Imported: Hilbert's Nullstellensatz, giving X_i^e = sum_j g_ij f_j with g_ij homogeneous of degree e - d
Remark 5.7: the dependence of C_1 on F is not straightforward; an explicit Nullstellensatz gives a very poor estimate
proofSteps: Fix a number field K containing the coordinates of P and the coefficients of all f_j; write |P|_v = max_i |x_i|_v, |F|_v for the maximum of the coefficients, and eps(v) = 1 for archimedean v and 0 otherwise.

Upper bound: the triangle inequality |t_1 + ... + t_n|_v <= n^{eps(v)} max |t_i|_v gives |f_j(P)|_v <= C^{eps(v)} |F|_v |P|_v^d; raise to n_v, multiply over v and take the [K:Q]-th root, using sum over archimedean v of n_v = [K:Q].
Lower bound: by the Nullstellensatz choose e >= 1 and g_ij with X_i^e = sum_j g_ij f_j; enlarge K to contain the coefficients of the g_ij.
Then |x_i|_v^e <= C^{eps(v)} max_j |g_ij(P)|_v |F(P)|_v and |g_ij(P)|_v <= C^{eps(v)} |G|_v |P|_v^{e-d}, so |P|_v^d <= C^{eps(v)} |G|_v |F(P)|_v.
Raise to n_v, multiply over v and take roots; e and H(G) do not depend on P.
acceptance: Check the lower bound fails for a rational map with a base point, e.g. [X_0^2, X_0 X_1] on P^1, at points approaching the base point.
Check that the constants are independent of P but not claimed to be effective in terms of F (Remark 5.7).

nodes.title: Theorem VIII.5.9: the height of the coefficient vector is comparable to the product of the heights of the roots
nodes.statement: If f(T) = a_0 T^d + ... + a_d = a_0 (T - alpha_1) ... (T - alpha_d) in Qbar[T] has degree d, then 2^{-d} prod_j H(alpha_j) <= H([a_0, ..., a_d]) <= 2^{d-1} prod_j H(alpha_j), where H(x) = H([x, 1]).
hypotheses: The inequality is unchanged by scaling f, so one may assume f monic
The proof uses eps(v) = 2 for archimedean v and 1 for nonarchimedean v, a different notation from the proof of Theorem 5.6
proofSteps: Reduce to a_0 = 1 and work over K = Q(alpha_1, ..., alpha_d).
Prove the local inequality eps(v)^{-d} prod_j max(|alpha_j|_v, 1) <= max_i |a_i|_v <= eps(v)^{d-1} prod_j max(|alpha_j|_v, 1) by induction on d; the case d = 1 is clear.
For the induction choose k with |alpha_k|_v maximal and write f = (T - alpha_k) g, so a_i = b_i - alpha_k b_{i-1}.
Upper bound: max |a_i|_v <= eps(v) max |b_i|_v max(|alpha_k|_v, 1), then apply the induction hypothesis to g.

Lower bound: if |alpha_k|_v <= eps(v) the bound is immediate; otherwise max |a_i|_v >= eps(v)^{-1} max |b_i|_v |alpha_k|_v (equality for nonarchimedean v, and (|alpha_k|_v - 1) max |b_i|_v > eps(v)^{-1} |alpha_k|_v max |b_i|_v for archimedean v), then induct.
Raise to n_v, multiply over v and take the [K:Q]-th root.
acceptance: Check the archimedean lower-bound step, where |alpha_k|_v > 2 is used.
Check on T^2 - 2 that the bounds 2^{-2} * 2 <= 2 <= 2 * 2 hold with H(sqrt 2) = sqrt 2.

sources.excerpt: We are going to prove that eps(v)^{-d} prod_{j=1}^{d} max{|alpha_j|_v, 1} <= max_{0<=i<=d} |a_i|_v <= eps(v)^{d-1} prod_{j=1}^{d} max{|alpha_j|_v, 1}.

nodes.title: Theorem VIII.5.11 (Northcott): finitely many points of bounded height and bounded degree
nodes.statement: For constants C and d, the set {P in P^N(Qbar) : H(P) <= C and [Q(P) : Q] <= d} is finite, where Q(P) is the minimal field of definition of P. In particular {P in P^N(K) : H_K(P) <= C} is finite for every number field K.
hypotheses: Q(P) is the minimal field of definition of P (Silverman I.2)
The base case K = Q, N arbitrary, is the count of at most (2C + 1)^{N+1} integer coordinate vectors (Example 5.1 and Remark 5.5)
Remark 5.12: an explicit bound on the number of points is easy to extract; Schanuel's asymptotic formula is cited, not proved
proofSteps: Choose coordinates with some x_j = 1, so Q(P) = Q(x_0, ..., x_N) and H_{Q(P)}(P) >= max_i H_{Q(P)}(x_i); hence it suffices to treat N = 1.
For x with H(x) <= C and e = [Q(x):Q] <= d, let f_x(T) = T^e + a_1 T^{e-1} + ... + a_e be its minimal polynomial over Q.
By Theorem 5.9 and Galois invariance (Theorem 5.10), H([1, a_1, ..., a_e]) <= 2^{e-1} H(x)^e <= (2C)^d.
The a_i are rational, so by the case K = Q there are finitely many possible f_x, each with at most d roots.
acceptance: State this as the finiteness input for the descent theorem: finiteness needs both bounded height and bounded degree.
Check that ampleness enters here only through the embedding in projective space: heights attached to a non-ample divisor do not have this property.

nodes.title: The height h_f on E(Kbar) for f in Kbar(E), and finiteness of K-points of bounded h_f (Proposition VIII.6.1)
nodes.statement: Let E/K be an elliptic curve over a number field and f a nonconstant function in K(E), viewed as a morphism f : E -> P^1. Define h_f(P) = h(f(P)) for P in E(Kbar), where h = log H is the absolute logarithmic height on P^1. Then for every constant C the set {P in E(K) : h_f(P) <= C} is finite.

Notation: f = g + O(1) means C_1 <= f - g <= C_2 on the relevant set
proofSteps: f maps E(K) to P^1(K) and is finite-to-one.
The image of the set lies in {Q in P^1(K) : H(Q) <= e^C}, which is finite by Theorem 5.11.

nodes.title: Theorem VIII.6.2 and Lemma VIII.6.3: h_f(P + Q) + h_f(P - Q) = 2h_f(P) + 2h_f(Q) + O(1) for even f, and comparison of even functions
nodes.statement: Let E/K be an elliptic curve and f in K(E) an even function (f o [-1] = f). Then h_f(P + Q) + h_f(P - Q) = 2h_f(P) + 2h_f(Q) + O(1) for all P, Q in E(Kbar), with the O(1) depending on E and f but not on P and Q. For even functions f, g in K(E), (deg g) h_f = (deg f) h_g + O(1); in particular h_f = (1/2)(deg f) h_x + O(1) for a Weierstrass coordinate x.
hypotheses: A Weierstrass equation y^2 = x^3 + Ax + B is chosen; this needs characteristic different from 2 and 3, which holds for number fields
The nonsingularity 4A^3 + 27B^2 != 0 is what makes the auxiliary map g : P^2 -> P^2 a morphism (page image: the identity is printed with "!= 0")
The subfield of even functions of K(E) is K(x) (Silverman III.2.3.1)
Cross-reference slip in the source: the proof announces "the next lemma (VIII.6.2)", which is Lemma 6.3
proofSteps: First take f = x. The cases P = O or Q = O are clear; otherwise write x(P) = x_1, x(Q) = x_2, x(P + Q) = x_3, x(P - Q) = x_4.
The addition formula gives x_3 + x_4 and x_3 x_4 as rational functions of x_1 + x_2 and x_1 x_2; define g([t, u, v]) = [u^2 - 4tv, 2u(At + v) + 4Bt^2, (v - At)^2 - 4Btu].
Let sigma : E x E -> P^2 send (P, Q) to [1, x(P) + x(Q), x(P)x(Q)] (via P^1 x P^1); then sigma o G = g o sigma for G(P, Q) = (P + Q, P - Q).

g is a morphism: a common zero with t = 0 forces u = v = 0; with t != 0 it gives a common root of psi(x) = 4x^3 + 4Ax + 4B and phi(x) = x^4 - 2Ax^2 - 8Bx + A^2, impossible since (12X^2 + 16A) phi - (3X^3 - 5AX - 27B) psi = 4(4A^3 + 27B^2) != 0.
Theorem 5.6 for the degree-2 morphism g gives h(sigma(P + Q, P - Q)) = 2h(sigma(P, Q)) + O(1).

Theorem 5.9 applied to (T + alpha_1)(T + alpha_2) gives h(alpha_1) + h(alpha_2) - log 4 <= h([1, alpha_1 + alpha_2, alpha_1 alpha_2]) <= h(alpha_1) + h(alpha_2) + log 2, i.e. h(sigma(R_1, R_2)) = h_x(R_1) + h_x(R_2) + O(1).
Lemma 6.3: an even f factors as r o x with r in K(X), so h_f = h_x o r = (deg r) h_x + O(1) by Theorem 5.6 and deg f = 2 deg r; compare two even functions through h_x.
Multiply the result for h_x by (1/2) deg f to obtain the theorem for arbitrary even f.
acceptance: Check the formulas for x_3 + x_4 and x_3 x_4 symbolically.

So P -> lambda_P is injective into the finite set of maps G_{L/K} -> E[m], and Phi is finite.

nodes.title: Proposition VIII.1.2 and VIII.2: the Kummer pairing E(K) x G_K -> E[m], its kernels, and the Kummer sequence
nodes.statement: Let E/K be an elliptic curve with E[m] contained in E(K). The Kummer pairing kappa(P, sigma) = Q^sigma - Q, for any Q in E(Kbar) with [m]Q = P, is (a) well defined, (b) bilinear, (c) has left kernel mE(K), and (d) has right kernel G_{Kbar/L}, where L = K([m]^{-1}E(K)) is the compositum of the fields K(Q) with [m]Q in E(K). Hence it induces a perfect bilinear pairing E(K)/mE(K) x G_{L/K} -> E[m], and L/K is Galois. Without the torsion assumption, Galois cohomology of 0 -> E[m] -> E(Kbar) -> E(Kbar) -> 0 gives the Kummer sequence 0 -> E(K)/mE(K) -> H^1(G_{Kbar/K}, E[m]) -> H^1(G_{Kbar/K}, E(Kbar))[m] -> 0, whose first map delta is represented by the cocycle sigma -> Q^sigma - Q.
hypotheses: E[m] contained in E(K) is needed for (a) and (b): it makes the value independent of the choice of Q and linear in sigma

For fields, Hilbert 90 makes delta : K^*/(K^*)^m -> H^1(G_{Kbar/K}, mu_m) an isomorphism (Proposition 2.2); for elliptic curves H^1(G, E(Kbar)) is not zero, which is the source of the Selmer/Shafarevich-Tate complication
Group cohomology facts (long exact sequence, inflation-restriction) are taken from Silverman Appendix B, which was not read
proofSteps: (a) [m](Q^sigma - Q) = P^sigma - P = O, and replacing Q by Q + T with T in E[m] contained in E(K) does not change Q^sigma - Q.
(b) Linearity in P is clear; kappa(P, sigma tau) = kappa(P, sigma)^tau + kappa(P, tau) and kappa(P, sigma) is fixed by tau.
(c) If P = [m]Q with Q in E(K) the pairing vanishes; conversely if kappa(P, .) = 0 then Q is Galois invariant, so Q in E(K).
(d) Elements of G_{Kbar/L} fix every such Q; conversely if kappa(P, sigma) = O for all P then sigma fixes every Q, hence fixes L.
L/K is Galois because G_{Kbar/L} is the kernel of sigma -> kappa(., sigma) in Hom(E(K), E[m]).
The Kummer sequence is the middle of the long exact cohomology sequence of multiplication by m; the connecting map is computed by the cocycle Q^sigma - Q, which is kappa(P, sigma).
acceptance: Check that without E[m] contained in E(K) the cocycle description of delta still holds but the pairing is no longer bilinear in sigma.

nodes.title: Proposition VIII.1.6: the maximal abelian extension of exponent m unramified outside a finite S is finite
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, S a finite set of places containing M_K^infinity, and m >= 2. The maximal abelian extension L/K of exponent m unramified outside S is a finite extension.
hypotheses: Imported from algebraic number theory: finiteness of the class group, Dirichlet's S-unit theorem (R_S^* finitely generated), and the main theorem of Kummer theory for fields containing mu_m (Silverman cites textbooks and Exercise 8.4)
The proof may enlarge K (to contain mu_m) and S (so that R_S is a principal ideal domain and v(m) = 0 outside S), since both only enlarge L
Remark 1.7: alternatively Minkowski's finiteness of extensions of bounded degree unramified outside S applies, since [K(Q):K] <= m^2
proofSteps: Reduce to mu_m contained in K and S large enough that R_S is a PID and v(m) = 0 for v not in S.
By Kummer theory L is the largest subfield of K(a^{1/m} : a in K^*) unramified outside S.
For v not in S, K_v(a^{1/m})/K_v is unramified if and only if ord_v(a) is divisible by m (the discriminant of X^m - a is +-m^m a^{m-1}).
So L = K(a^{1/m} : a in T_S), where T_S = {a in K^*/(K^*)^m : ord_v(a) = 0 mod m for all v not in S}.
Since R_S is a PID, aR_S = b^m R_S and a = u b^m with u in R_S^*, so R_S^*/(R_S^*)^m surjects onto T_S.
R_S^* is finitely generated (Dirichlet), so T_S and hence L/K are finite.

nodes.title: Lemma VIII.9.5, Proposition VIII.9.6 and Corollary VIII.9.7: hhat extends to a positive definite quadratic form on E(K) (x) R, and the elliptic regulator is positive
nodes.statement: Let E/K be an elliptic curve over a number field. The canonical height extends to a positive definite quadratic form on the finite-dimensional real vector space E(K) (x) R, in which E(K)/E_tors(K) is a lattice. With the canonical height pairing <P, Q> = hhat(P + Q) - hhat(P) - hhat(Q) and generators P_1, ..., P_r of E(K)/E_tors(K), the elliptic regulator R_{E/K} = det(<P_i, P_j>) (1 if r = 0) satisfies R_{E/K} > 0.
hypotheses: Needs the Mordell-Weil theorem, so that E(K) (x) R is finite-dimensional and E(K)/E_tors(K) is a lattice
Remark 9.4 (Cassels): positivity on the lattice (Theorem 9.3(c)(d)) does not by itself give positive definiteness on E(K) (x) R; the finiteness of bounded-height sets is also needed
Imported: diagonalization of a real quadratic form and Minkowski's convex body theorem
Remark 9.8: the regulator relative to K differs from R_{E/K} by [K:Q]^r
proofSteps: Lemma 9.5: let q be a quadratic form on V with lattice L such that (i) q(P) = 0 on L only for P = 0 and (ii) {P in L : q(P) <= C} is finite for all C.
Diagonalize q = x_1^2 + ... + x_s^2 - x_{s+1}^2 - ... - x_{s+t}^2 with s + t <= r; by (i) and (ii), lambda = inf{q(P) : P in L, P != 0} > 0.

If s < r, the convex symmetric set B(lambda/2, delta) = {sum_{i<=s} x_i^2 <= lambda/2, sum x_{s+i}^2 <= delta} has volume tending to infinity with delta, so by Minkowski it contains a nonzero lattice point P with q(P) <= lambda/2, a contradiction.
Proposition 9.6: condition (i) is Theorem 9.3(c)(d); condition (ii) follows from Theorem 9.3(e) and Proposition 6.1.
Corollary 9.7: the Gram determinant of a basis of a lattice for a positive definite form is positive.

nodes.title: Poonen Theorem 8.4.1: the fibres of the evaluation map X(k) -> H^1(k, G) of a torsor are the images of the twisted torsors
nodes.statement: Let k be a field, X a k-variety, G a smooth affine algebraic group over k, f : Z -> X a G-torsor with class zeta in H^1(X, G) (fppf), and for x in X(k) let zeta(x) in H^1(k, G) be the class of the fibre Z_x. For tau in H^1(k, G) let f^tau : Z^tau -> X be the twisted torsor Z^tau = Z x^G T (T a torsor representing tau), a torsor under the inner twist G^tau. Then {x in X(k) : zeta(x) = tau} = f^tau(Z^tau(k)); in particular X(k) is the disjoint union over tau in H^1(k, G) of f^tau(Z^tau(k)).
hypotheses: G-torsor means a right fppf G_X-torsor over X; H^1(X, G) is the Cech fppf pointed set, in bijection with isomorphism classes of torsors (Poonen Theorem 6.5.10(i), not read)
Imported: Proposition 5.12.14 (a torsor is trivial if and only if it has a rational point) and the construction of twists (Example 6.5.12, read)

Convention check (page images pp. 183 and 240): Example 6.5.12 prints Z^tau := Z x^G T, while the subtraction of torsors in 6.5.6.4 and the proof of Theorem 8.4.1 use Z x^G T^{-1}. A contracted product with the right G-torsor T needs the left G-space T^{-1}, so the T^{-1} form is the consistent one
proofSteps: x lies in f^tau(Z^tau(k)) if and only if the fibre Z^tau_x is a trivial G^tau-torsor (Proposition 5.12.14).
The fibre Z^tau_x is the contracted product Z_x x^G T^{-1}, which is a trivial G^tau-torsor if and only if Z_x is isomorphic to T as G-torsors (take the contracted product with T on the right).
That is exactly zeta(x) = tau.
acceptance: Check the right-action conventions for the contracted product in the twist.
Check the example of Section 8.3: the degree-2 covering Z -> X with G = Z/2Z and twists Z_c indexed by c in Q^*/Q^*2.

nodes.title: Poonen Theorem 6.5.13: H^1_S(k, G) has finite fibres over prod_{v in S} H^1(k_v, F), and is finite over a number field
nodes.statement: Let k be a global field, S a finite nonempty set of places containing the archimedean ones, G a smooth finite-type affine group scheme over O_{k,S} with generic fibre G, and 1 -> G^0 -> G -> F -> 1 the connected-component sequence (spread out, F finite etale of order n). Let H^1_S(k, G) be the set of classes unramified outside S. Then (a) the maps H^1_S(k, G) -> H^1_S(k, F) -> prod_{v in S} H^1(k_v, F) have finite fibres, and (b) if k is a number field, H^1_S(k, G) is finite.
hypotheses: tau is unramified at v if tau_v comes from H^1(O_v, G); the equivalence with coming from H^1(O_{k,v}, G) is cited to BLR 6.2 Proposition D.4(b)

Imported (stated with citations, proofs not read): Lang's theorem H^1(finite field, connected group) = 0 (Theorem 5.12.19(a)); Hensel's lemma (Theorem 3.5.63(a)); Borel-Serre finiteness of the fibres of H^1(k, G) -> prod_{v not in S} H^1(k_v, G) for affine G (Theorem 5.12.29); a variant of Hermite's theorem on extensions of bounded degree and discriminant ([Ser97, 4.1]); finiteness of H^1(k_v, F) for local fields of characteristic 0 (Borel-Serre, Theorem 5.12.24(a))
Part (b) needs characteristic 0: over local fields of characteristic p, H^1(k_v, Z/pZ) is infinite (Warning 5.12.25)
proofSteps: Step 1: for v not in S, H^1(O_v, F) -> H^1(k_v, F) has trivial kernel, because an F-torsor over O_v is finite, hence proper, so T(O_v) = T(k_v).
Step 2: H^1(O_v, G^0) = 0: the special fibre of a G^0-torsor has a point by Lang's theorem and lifts by Hensel's lemma since the torsor is smooth.
Step 3: the kernel of h : H^1_S(k, G) -> H^1_S(k, F) lies in the Shafarevich-Tate set Sha^1_S(k, G), which is finite by Theorem 5.12.29.
Step 4: every fibre of h is finite, by twisting (subtraction of tau and of phi) to reduce to the kernel for G^tau.

Step 5: an F-torsor class unramified outside S with fixed local classes at S is split by the compositum k' of the finitely many extensions of degree <= n unramified outside S with bounded discriminant at S (Hermite); inflation-restriction with finite Gal(k'/k) and F(k') gives finiteness.
Step 6: over a number field each H^1(k_v, F), v in S, is finite, so (a) gives (b).
acceptance: Check Step 5's use of Hermite's theorem with bounded discriminant at the places of S, not unramifiedness.
Check that (b) is stated only for number fields.

nodes.title: Poonen Definition 8.4.4, Proposition 8.4.2 and Theorem 8.4.6: the Selmer set Sel_Z(k, G) is finite for proper X
nodes.statement: Let k be a global field, X a k-variety, G a smooth affine algebraic group and f : Z -> X a G-torsor. The Selmer set is Sel_Z(k, G) = {tau in H^1(k, G) : tau_v in image(X(k_v) -> H^1(k_v, G)) for all places v}; equivalently the set of tau with Z^tau(k_v) nonempty for all v, and X(k) is the disjoint union over tau in Sel_Z(k, G) of f^tau(Z^tau(k)). If X is proper, then Sel_Z(k, G) is finite.
hypotheses: Proposition 8.4.2 (local input): for a local field k, a proper k-variety X, a finite etale group F and an F-torsor, the image of X(k) -> H^1(k, F) is finite (Krasner's lemma makes the evaluation map locally constant; X(k) is compact)
Imported: spreading out (Theorem 3.2.1) and the valuative criterion for properness; Theorem 6.5.13(a)
Remark 8.4.7 asserts that Sel_Z(k, G) is effectively computable even without knowing X(k); no proof is given in this source
Remark 8.4.5: for an isogeny of abelian varieties viewed as a torsor under its kernel, this is the usual Selmer group, e.g. the 2-Selmer group of Silverman X.4
proofSteps: Let F be the component group of G; choose S so that G, X (proper) and Z spread out over O_{k,S}.
For v not in S, a point of X(k_v) extends to X(O_v) by the valuative criterion, so tau_v comes from H^1(O_v, G); hence Sel_Z(k, G) is contained in H^1_S(k, G).
For v in S the image of X(k_v) -> H^1(k_v, F) is finite (Proposition 8.4.2), so the image of Sel_Z(k, G) in prod_{v in S} H^1(k_v, F) is finite.
Theorem 6.5.13(a) then gives finiteness of Sel_Z(k, G).
acceptance: Check that properness is used twice: for integral points at v not in S and for compactness of X(k_v) at v in S.
Keep Remark 8.4.7 (computability) separate from the proved finiteness.

nodes.title: Poonen Corollary 8.4.8 (Chevalley-Weil form): a finite separable k' with X(k) contained in f(Z(k'))
nodes.statement: Let k be a global field, X a proper k-variety, G a smooth affine algebraic group and f : Z -> X a G-torsor. There is a finite separable extension k' of k such that X(k) is contained in f(Z(k')).
hypotheses: Uses the finiteness of Sel_Z(k, G) (Theorem 8.4.6) and X(k) = union over tau in Sel_Z of f^tau(Z^tau(k))

For a finite etale G this is the uniform field of definition of fibres used in the Parshin construction (RP.4); a non-Galois etale cover must first be replaced by a torsor, which this source does not discuss
proofSteps: Each tau in H^1(k, G) becomes trivial over some finite separable extension.
Take a compositum k' trivializing the finitely many tau in Sel_Z(k, G).
Over k', each twist Z^tau -> X becomes isomorphic to Z -> X, so f^tau(Z^tau(k)) is contained in f(Z(k')).
acceptance: Check that k' depends on Z -> X but not on the point x.
For a finite etale G, compare with the Hermite-Minkowski form in Faltings Lemma 4: the fibres over rational points are etale algebras of bounded degree unramified outside a fixed S.

nodes.title: Poonen Theorem 8.4.9: A(k)/mA(k) is finite for an abelian variety over a global field and char k not dividing m
nodes.statement: Let A be an abelian variety over a global field k and m a positive integer not divisible by char k. Then A(k)/mA(k) is finite. Poonen Theorem 5.7.31 (Mordell-Weil for abelian varieties: A(k) finitely generated) is only sketched: it combines this with the theory of height functions, cited to Serre, Lectures on the Mordell-Weil theorem, 4.3.
hypotheses: Proposition 5.7.4: [m] : A -> A is etale when char k does not divide m (proof sketched: the derivative at 0 is multiplication by m; invertibility needs char k not dividing m)
A[m] is then a finite etale, hence smooth affine, group scheme and [m] : A -> A is an A[m]-torsor
"One checks that the two maps A(k) -> H^1(k, A[m]) coincide": asserted in the source, not proved
fppf cohomology would be needed when char k divides m (the roadmap asks for it); this source excludes that case
The height-function part of the Mordell-Weil theorem for abelian varieties is not in the sources read (Serre, Lectures on the Mordell-Weil theorem, and Hindry-Silverman Part C are unread)
proofSteps: [m] : A -> A is etale (Proposition 5.7.4), giving the exact sequence of etale sheaves 0 -> A[m] -> A -> A -> 0 and the coboundary A(k) -> H^1(k, A[m]) with kernel mA(k).
Viewing [m] as an A[m]-torsor gives an evaluation map a -> class of [m]^{-1}(a), whose image lies in the Selmer set Sel_A(k, A[m]).
A is proper, so the Selmer set is finite (Theorem 8.4.6).
The two maps coincide, so A(k)/mA(k) is isomorphic to the image of the evaluation map, which is finite.
acceptance: Compare with Silverman VIII.1 for elliptic curves: the same finiteness through Kummer theory instead of Selmer sets.
Record that the proof covers global function fields when char k does not divide m, and says nothing when char k divides m.

nodes.title: Silverman X.4: the phi-Selmer group, the Shafarevich-Tate group, the exact sequence and finiteness of the Selmer group
nodes.statement: Let phi : E -> E' be an isogeny of elliptic curves over a number field K. Define S^(phi)(E/K) = ker(H^1(G_{Kbar/K}, E[phi]) -> prod_v WC(E/K_v)) and Sha(E/K) = ker(WC(E/K) -> prod_v WC(E/K_v)). Then (a) 0 -> E'(K)/phi(E(K)) -> S^(phi)(E/K) -> Sha(E/K)[phi] -> 0 is exact, and (b) S^(phi)(E/K) is finite. More precisely, S^(phi)(E/K) is contained in H^1(G_{Kbar/K}, E[phi]; S) for S containing the archimedean places, the places of bad reduction and the places dividing deg phi, and for a finite G-module M, H^1(G_{Kbar/K}, M; S) is finite.
hypotheses: WC(E/K) is identified with H^1(G_{Kbar/K}, E) by (X.3.6), which was not read
Remark 4.1.1: the definitions do not depend on the chosen extensions of v to Kbar

Remark 4.5: the Selmer group is effectively computable, because H^1(G, E[phi]; S) is and local solubility of each homogeneous space reduces to a finite computation by Hensel's lemma; this is argued in prose, not as a theorem
Isogenous curves have the same bad primes (VII.7.2, not read)
proofSteps: Take Galois cohomology of 0 -> E[phi] -> E -> E' -> 0 over K and over each K_v, giving the diagram (**) of short exact sequences.
(a) follows from the diagram and the definitions.
(b) For v not dividing m = deg phi with good reduction and xi in S^(phi), xi is trivial in WC(E/K_v), so xi_sigma = P^sigma - P for some P in E(Kbar_v).
For sigma in inertia, P^sigma - P reduces to O and lies in E[phi], contained in E[m], so it is O by VIII.1.4; hence xi is unramified outside S.

Lemma 4.3: for finite M, pass to a finite extension trivializing the action (inflation-restriction); then H^1(G, M; S) = Hom(G, M; S) factors through the maximal abelian extension of exponent m unramified outside S, finite by VIII.1.6.
acceptance: Check that for phi = [m] the sequence gives E(K)/mE(K) as a subgroup of the finite S^(m)(E/K), recovering the weak Mordell-Weil theorem.
Keep the upper bound E'(K)/phi(E(K)) <= S^(phi)(E/K) separate from equality, which fails exactly when Sha(E/K)[phi] is nonzero.

nodes.title: Silverman Theorem X.1.1 and Proposition X.1.4: the pairing b(P, T), the injection E(K)/2E(K) -> K(S,2) x K(S,2) and its homogeneous-space criterion
nodes.statement: Let E/K have E[m] contained in E(K). There is a bilinear pairing b : E(K)/mE(K) x E[m] -> K^*/(K^*)^m with e_m(delta_E(P), T) = delta_K(b(P, T)), nondegenerate on the left, with image in K(S, m) = {b : ord_v(b) = 0 mod m for all v not in S} (S = infinite places, bad primes, primes dividing m), computed by b(P, T) = f_T(P) mod (K^*)^m where div(f_T) = m(T) - m(O) and f_T o [m] = g_T^m. For m = 2 and E : y^2 = (x - e_1)(x - e_2)(x - e_3) with e_i in K, the map P = (x, y) -> (x - e_1, x - e_2) (with the stated values at O, (e_1, 0), (e_2, 0)) is an injective homomorphism E(K)/2E(K) -> K(S, 2) x K(S, 2), and a pair (b_1, b_2) not in the image of O, (e_1, 0), (e_2, 0) comes from a point if and only if b_1 z_1^2 - b_2 z_2^2 = e_2 - e_1 and b_1 z_1^2 - b_1 b_2 z_3^2 = e_3 - e_1 have a solution (z_1, z_2, z_3) in K^* x K^* x K, in which case P = (b_1 z_1^2 + e_1, b_1 b_2 z_1 z_2 z_3).
hypotheses: Imported: the Weil pairing e_m and its bilinearity and nondegeneracy (III.8.1, not read); E[m] contained in E(K) implies mu_m contained in K
Hilbert 90 for mu_m (B.2.5c) gives delta_K : K^*/(K^*)^m -> Hom(G_{Kbar/K}, mu_m)
The m = 2 functions are f_T = x - e, which requires the explicit duplication formula for x o [2] (checked "by a calculation" in the source)
b(T, T) is computed by linearity: b(T_1, T_1) = (e_1 - e_3)/(e_1 - e_2) and b(T_2, T_2) = (e_2 - e_3)/(e_2 - e_1)
proofSteps: (a) Well defined by Hilbert 90; bilinear from bilinearity of kappa and of e_m.
(b) If b(P, T) = 1 for all T, then e_m(kappa(P, sigma), T) = 1 for all T and sigma, so kappa(P, .) = 0 by nondegeneracy of e_m and P is in mE(K) by VIII.1.2(c).
(c) K(b(P, T)^{1/m}) is contained in L = K([m]^{-1}E(K)), unramified outside S (VIII.1.5(b)); for v not dividing m, K(beta)/K is unramified at v iff ord_v(beta^m) = 0 mod m.
(d) With P = [m]Q and b(P, T) = beta^m, g_T(Q)^sigma / g_T(Q) = beta^sigma / beta, so f_T(P) = g_T(Q)^m = beta^m mod (K^*)^m.
For m = 2, substitute b_1 z_1^2 = x - e_1, b_2 z_2^2 = x - e_2, y = b_1 b_2 z_1 z_2 z_3 and eliminate x to get the two quadratic equations.
acceptance: Check that the image of E(K)/2E(K) is contained in the finite, explicitly computable group K(S, 2) x K(S, 2) (Remark 1.2).

Check the note that local insolubility of the homogeneous spaces is easy to test, while a locally soluble space without global points is the failure of the Hasse principle that makes the method ineffective (Remark 1.2).

nodes.title: Silverman Example X.1.5 and Example X.4.5.1: E(Q) = Z x Z/2Z x Z/2Z for y^2 = x^3 - 12x^2 + 20x, with local conditions at R and Q_5 and a corrected Selmer rank
nodes.statement: For E : y^2 = x^3 - 12x^2 + 20x = x(x - 2)(x - 10) over Q, with Delta = 409600 = 2^14 5^2, S = {2, 5, infinity} and Q(S, 2) = {+-1, +-2, +-5, +-10}: (1) E_tors(Q) = E[2], since #E~(F_3) = 4; (2) the torsion points O, (0, 0), (2, 0), (10, 0) map to (1, 1), (5, -2), (2, -1), (10, 2); (3) (1, -3) in E(Q) maps to (1, -1), giving the further points (20, 60), (18, -48), (10/9, -80/27); (4) every other pair is excluded by real or 5-adic insolubility of b_1 z_1^2 - b_2 z_2^2 = 2, b_1 z_1^2 - b_1 b_2 z_3^2 = 10; so the image of E(Q)/2E(Q) is the 8-element group of Q-trivial pairs and E(Q) = Z x Z/2Z x Z/2Z. Consequently S^(2)(E/Q) = (Z/2Z)^3 and Sha(E/Q)[2] = 0.
hypotheses: Correction: Example X.4.5.1 (p. 335, page image) prints S^(2)(E/Q) = (Z/2Z)^2 for this curve. Table 10.1 (p. 317, page image) has eight Q-trivial pairs, and E(Q) = Z x Z/2Z x Z/2Z gives E(Q)/2E(Q) = (Z/2Z)^3, which injects into S^(2)(E/Q). So (Z/2Z)^2 cannot be right, and with Sha[2] = 0 the value is (Z/2Z)^3
The text layer of note 6 reads "b_1 = 0 (mod 5)"; the page image prints b_1 not congruent to 0 and b_2 congruent to 0 (mod 5)
The step from E(Q)/2E(Q) = (Z/2Z)^3 and E_tors(Q) = E[2] to E(Q) = Z x (Z/2Z)^2 uses the Mordell-Weil theorem
Torsion injects into the reduction mod 3 by VII.3.5 (not read)
proofSteps: Compute the image of E[2] with Proposition X.1.4.
Real place: b_1 < 0 < b_2 makes the first equation insoluble over R; b_1, b_2 < 0 makes the second insoluble over R.

Q_5: if 5 does not divide b_1 and 5 divides b_2, then z_1, z_2 are 5-integral, then z_1 = 0 mod 5, giving 0 = 2 mod 5; for (b_1, b_2) = (1, 2), 2 is a non-residue mod 5, so z_1 = z_3 = 0 mod 5 and 0 = 10 mod 25.
Multiplying Q_5-insoluble pairs by Q-trivial pairs fills the table; since the map is a homomorphism, the image is the group of eight Q-trivial pairs.
Conclude E(Q)/2E(Q) = (Z/2Z)^3; with E_tors(Q) = (Z/2Z)^2 and finite generation, E(Q) = Z x (Z/2Z)^2.
Every Selmer element is realized by a point, so Sha(E/Q)[2] = 0 and S^(2)(E/Q) = E(Q)/2E(Q) = (Z/2Z)^3.
acceptance: This is the elliptic 2-descent acceptance example of RP.1: local conditions at R and Q_5, the global image (eight pairs), and a proved finite-generation conclusion with rank 1.

nodes.title: Silverman Proposition X.4.9 and Example X.4.10: descent via 2-isogeny, and E(Q) = Z x Z/2Z for y^2 = x^3 - 6x^2 + 17x
nodes.statement: Let E : y^2 = x^3 + ax^2 + bx and E' : Y^2 = X^3 - 2aX^2 + (a^2 - 4b)X, with the 2-isogeny phi(x, y) = (y^2/x^2, y(b - x^2)/x^2) of kernel {O, (0, 0)}, S = M_K^infinity union {v : v(2) != 0 or v(b) != 0 or v(a^2 - 4b) != 0}, and C_d : dw^2 = d^2 - 2adz^2 + (a^2 - 4b)z^4. nodes.title: Poonen Section 8.1: the F-obstruction set X(A)^F, its functoriality, and the replacement of Br A by the direct sum of the Br k_v
nodes.statement: Let k be a global field with adele ring A, F : (Schemes_k)^opp -> Sets a functor and X a k-variety. For A in F(X) and a k-algebra L, evaluation gives ev_A : X(L) -> F(L), compatible with X(k) -> X(A) and F(k) -> F(A). Let X(A)^A be the set of adelic points whose image in F(A) comes from F(k), and X(A)^F = intersection over A in F(X) of X(A)^A. Then X(k) is contained in X(A)^F. If X(A) is nonempty but X(A)^F is empty, there is an F-obstruction to the local-global principle, and then X(k) is empty; if X(prod k_v)^F != X(prod k_v) there is an F-obstruction to weak approximation. The functor Br gives the Brauer set X(A)^Br and F = H^1(-, G) for an affine algebraic group G gives X(A)^{H^1(X,G)}. Functoriality (Proposition 8.1.8): for pi : X' -> X, (pi^*A)(x') = A(pi(x')); hence X -> X(A)^F is functorial, and if F(X) -> F(X') is surjective then X'(A)^F is the inverse image of X(A)^F.

nodes.statement: The affine curve y^2 = (x^2 + 1)(x^4 + 1) over Q has exactly the six rational points (0, +-1), (1, +-2), (-1, +-2). The method: for coprime X, Z with Y^2 = (X^2 + Z^2)(X^4 + Z^4) the two factors have common prime divisors only at 2, so X^4 + Z^4 = cW^2 with c in {1, 2}; the twists Z_c : y^2 = (x^2 + 1)(x^4 + 1), cw^2 = x^4 + 1 of the etale double cover Z -> X satisfy X(Q) = union of f_c(Z_c(Q)), and only c in {1, 2} have points everywhere locally. The genus-1 curves Y_c : cw^2 = x^4 + 1 are birational to the elliptic curves 32A2 : y^2 = x^3 - x and 64A1 : y^2 = x^3 - 4x, both of rank 0 with torsion Z/2Z x Z/2Z, so each has four rational points; the fibres of Z_c -> Y_c over them give Z_c(Q) and hence X(Q). Z -> X is etale and Galois with group Z/2Z (Proposition 8.3.4).

X is the nice genus-2 curve with two rational points at infinity; finiteness of X(Q) is Faltings' theorem, not used by the method
Remark 8.3.2: the Jacobian of X is isogenous to E x E with rank 2 = g, so Chabauty's method does not apply directly; the Demyanenko-Manin method could
Proposition 8.3.4 needs Z -> X etale between nice curves with k(Z)/k(X) Galois
proofSteps: A prime dividing X^2 + Z^2 and X^4 + Z^4 divides 2Z^4 and 2X^4, hence equals 2 since gcd(X, Z) = 1.
So X^4 + Z^4 = cW^2 with c in {+-1, +-2}, and c > 0 because the left side is positive; this discards the twists with c < 0 (no real points).
For c in {1, 2}, points of Y_c(Q) are torsion points of rank-0 elliptic curves: x = 0 on Y_1 and x = +-1 on Y_2.
Z -> X is etale: over the opens where x^4 + 1, respectively x^2 + 1, is nonvanishing the cover adjoins a square root of a unit; similarly at infinity.
Proposition 8.3.4: the Galois action on k(Z) gives Z x G -> Z x_X Z, an isomorphism generically, hence everywhere for smooth proper curves.
acceptance: This is RP.3's acceptance example of a torsor with no rational lift: the twists Z_c with c < 0 have no real points.

nodes.title: Poonen Theorem 8.4.10 and Corollary 8.4.11 (Minchev): a nontrivial finite etale cover prevents strong approximation
nodes.statement: Let k be a global field, S a finite set of places and f : Y -> X a finite etale morphism of geometrically integral k-varieties. If X(A^S) is nonempty and f is not an isomorphism, then X(k) is not dense in X(A^S), i.e. X fails strong approximation with respect to S. Consequently (Corollary 8.4.11), a normal geometrically integral k-variety X with X(A^S) nonempty whose base change to k^s is not algebraically simply connected fails strong approximation with respect to S. Normality is needed (Remark 8.4.12: a nodal cubic with irrational tangent slopes satisfies strong approximation).
hypotheses: Imported, not read: spreading out (Theorem 3.2.1), Krasner's lemma (Proposition 3.5.74), Hensel's lemma (Theorem 3.5.63(a)), the Lang-Weil estimate #X(F_v) = q_v^n + O(q_v^{n-1/2}) (Theorem 7.7.1(ii)), Lemma 3.5.57 producing a nontrivial geometrically integral finite etale cover
The "finitely many possibilities for F^{-1}(x)" step uses finiteness of finite etale O_{k,S}-algebras of bounded degree with bounded ramification over S, stated without further citation
Minchev's original theorem is over number fields; Poonen extends it to global fields
proofSteps: Let d = deg f > 1; enlarge S so that f spreads out to a finite etale F : Y -> X over O_{k,S} with geometrically integral fibres and X(O_v) nonempty for v not in S.

As x runs over X(O_{k,S}), the finite etale O_{k,S}-scheme F^{-1}(x) has bounded degree and bounded ramification over S (Krasner at v in S), so there are finitely many possibilities; hence infinitely many v not in S split in F^{-1}(x) for every x.
By Lang-Weil, #Y'(F_w) < d #X'(F_w) for some such w, so some point of X'(F_w) does not split in Y'; lift it by Hensel to a_w in X'(O_w).

By Krasner, U_w = {u_w : F^{-1}(u_w) isomorphic to F^{-1}(a_w)} is open; the open set U_w x prod_{v not in S, v != w} X(O_v) of X(A^S) contains no rational point, since a rational point in it would lie in X(O_{k,S}) and w would both split and not split in its fibre.
Corollary 8.4.11: if X(k) is empty strong approximation fails by definition; otherwise Lemma 3.5.57 gives a nontrivial geometrically integral finite etale cover.
acceptance: Check the role of normality with the nodal cubic of Remark 8.4.12.
Separate this integral-point obstruction from the rational-point descent obstruction of Section 8.4.7.

nodes.title: Faltings Lemma 4 as used in Satz 7, and Poonen Corollary 8.4.8: one finite extension K_1 over which every fibre above a K-point splits
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, X/K a smooth projective curve and phi : X_1 -> X an unramified covering of degree m. There is a finite extension K_1 of K such that for every x in X(K) the fibre phi^{-1}(x) consists of m distinct K_1-rational points. Faltings obtains K_1 from Lemma 4: for a finite set S of places of K there are only finitely many extensions K'/K of given degree unramified outside S (Hermite-Minkowski). In torsor form (Poonen Corollary 8.4.8): for a torsor f : Z -> X under a smooth affine group over a proper X there is a finite separable k' with X(k) contained in f(Z(k')).
hypotheses: Faltings states only "Lemma 4 liefert einen endlichen Oberkoerper K_1"; the intermediate facts are not written. They are: phi and X_1, X have smooth models over O_{K,S} with phi etale, so for x in X(K) the fibre is a finite etale O_{K,S}-algebra; hence its residue fields have degree <= m over K and are unramified outside S; then Hermite-Minkowski applies and K_1 is their compositum
Poonen's Corollary 8.4.8 proves the torsor case; a covering that is not Galois must first be replaced by its Galois closure, which neither source discusses
Lemma 4 itself is proved in the source only as "Bekannt (Hermite-Minkowski)"
proofSteps: Spread X_1 -> X out to a finite etale morphism of smooth proper curves over O_{K,S} for a finite S (not written in Faltings).
For x in X(K), x extends to an O_{K,S}-point (properness), and the pullback of the cover is finite etale over O_{K,S} of degree m.
So each point of phi^{-1}(x) is defined over an extension of degree <= m unramified outside S.
Lemma 4 (Hermite-Minkowski): there are finitely many such extensions; let K_1 be their compositum.
Torsor version: Sel_Z(k, G) is finite (Theorem 8.4.6); trivialize its elements over one compositum (Corollary 8.4.8).
acceptance: This is the "field extension is uniformly controlled" part of RP.4's acceptance: K_1 depends on phi and S, not on x.

nodes.title: Faltings Satz 7 (Parshin's argument): rational points x give auxiliary curves Y(x) with bad reduction in a fixed finite set, so Korollar 1 to Satz 6 gives finiteness of X(K)
nodes.statement: Let X/K be a smooth curve of genus g >= 2 over a number field. After possibly extending K there is an unramified covering phi : X_1 -> X of degree m > 2. With K_1 as in the uniform field lemma, for x in X(K) choose y in phi^{-1}(x), let D = phi^{-1}(x) - {y} and A/K_1 the generalized Jacobian of (X_1, D), and use y to map X_1 - D to A. Multiplication by 2 on A induces a covering Y(x) -> X_1 ramified exactly over D, and Y(x) has bad reduction only at places v of K_1 with (a) v | 2, (b) X_1 bad at v, or (c) phi ramified in the fibre mod v. These are finitely many places independent of x, so by the finiteness of curves with good reduction outside a finite set there are finitely many possibilities for Y(x), and likewise for the composite Y(x) -> X_1 -> X, which is ramified exactly over x. Hence X(K) is finite (Mordell conjecture, Faltings' theorem). All known proofs are ineffective (Poonen Remark 9.5.2).
hypotheses: Page image p. 365: the covering degree is printed "m > 2" and the genus bound "g >= 2"; m > 2 makes D contain at least two points

Not written in the source and needed: existence of the unramified covering after a field extension (e.g. from the Jacobian of X); the construction of the generalized Jacobian of (X_1, D) and of the map X_1 - D -> A; that the pullback of [2] is geometrically connected and ramified exactly over D; the bad-reduction bound for Y(x); that Y(x) has genus at least 2; and finiteness of the maps Y(x) -> X for fixed Y(x) (de Franchis-type), used in "Dasselbe gilt fuer die Abbildung Y(x) -> X_1 -> X"
The finiteness input is Korollar 1 to Satz 6 (curves of genus >= 2 with good reduction outside S), whose proof in the source is the single word "Torelli"

Poonen Theorem 9.5.1 states the theorem without proof ("the known proofs are very complicated") and records Parshin's reduction to Shafarevich's conjecture; Vojta and Bombieri gave Diophantine-approximation proofs (not read)
Poonen Remark 9.5.2: all known proofs are ineffective; no algorithm listing X(K) is known
proofSteps: Choose phi : X_1 -> X unramified of degree m > 2, after extending K.
Choose K_1 uniformly (uniform field lemma), and for x in X(K) a point y in phi^{-1}(x), all defined over K_1.
Form D = phi^{-1}(x) - {y}, the generalized Jacobian A of (X_1, D) and the map X_1 - D -> A based at y.
Pull back multiplication by 2 on A to get Y(x) -> X_1, ramified exactly over D, with bad reduction only at the places (a)-(c).
Apply finiteness of curves with good reduction outside the fixed finite set of places of K_1: finitely many Y(x) up to isomorphism.
For each Y(x), finitely many composites Y(x) -> X, and the branch point of the composite recovers x; so X(K) is finite.
acceptance: Check the uniform control required by RP.4: degree m and cover phi fixed, K_1 fixed, bad set (a)-(c) fixed, and all independent of x.

nodes.title: Silverman IX.1-IX.2: Roth's theorem (approximation exponent 2 + epsilon over number fields), v-adic distance on curves, invariance under unramified maps, and Corollary IX.2.4
nodes.statement: Roth (Theorem IX.1.4, stated): every number field K has approximation exponent tau(d) = 2 + epsilon: for alpha in Kbar, v in M_K extended to K(alpha) and any C, only finitely many x in K satisfy |x - alpha|_v < C H_K(x)^{-2-epsilon}. For a curve C/K, v in M_K and Q in C(K_v), set d_v(P, Q) = min(|t_Q(P)|_v^{1/e}, 1) for a function t_Q with a zero of order e >= 1 at Q and no other zeros. Then (Proposition 2.2) log|F(P)|_v / log d_v(P, Q) -> ord_Q(F) as P -> Q v-adically, independently of t_Q; (Proposition 2.3) for a finite map phi : C_1 -> C_2, log d_v(phi(P), phi(Q)) / log d_v(P, Q) -> e_phi(Q); and (Corollary 2.4) for nonconstant f in K(C) and Q in C(Kbar), liminf over P in C(K), P -> Q of log d_v(P, Q) / log H_K(f(P)) >= -2.
hypotheses: Roth's theorem is not proved in the source: Section IX.8 sketches the proof and the general case is cited to Hindry-Silverman Part D and Lang, Fundamentals of Diophantine Geometry, Chapter 7
Remark 1.6: Roth's theorem, and hence every finiteness result of IX.2-IX.3, is ineffective
t_Q exists by Riemann-Roch (footnote on p. 273)
If Q is not a v-adic accumulation point of C(K) the liminf is defined to be 0
proofSteps: Proposition 2.2: phi = F^e / t_Q^f has neither zero nor pole at Q, so |phi(P)|_v is bounded away from 0 and infinity near Q, and the limit is f = ord_Q F.
Proposition 2.3: (t_{phi(Q)} o phi)^{e_1} / t_Q^{e_phi(Q) e_2} has neither zero nor pole at Q; take logarithms.
Corollary 2.4: replacing f by 1/f, assume f(Q) finite; f - f(Q) vanishes to order e at Q, so log d_v(P, Q) / log H_K(f(P)) = (1/e) log|f(P) - f(Q)|_v / log H_K(f(P)) asymptotically.
Roth with tau = 2 + epsilon gives H_K(f(P))^tau |f(P) - f(Q)|_v >= 1 for all but finitely many P, so the liminf is >= -(2 + epsilon)/e >= -(2 + epsilon); let epsilon -> 0.
acceptance: Keep Roth's theorem as an explicit import with its exact form: number field K, arbitrary absolute value v, alpha of any degree over K.
Check that Proposition 2.3 measures ramification, not degree (contrast with Theorem VIII.5.6).

Then lim over P in E(K) with h_f(P) -> infinity of log d_v(P, Q) / h_f(P) = 0. Consequently (Corollary 3.2.1), for Weierstrass coordinates x, y and a finite set S of places containing the archimedean ones, {P in E(K) : x(P) in R_S} is finite.

proofSteps: Pick P_i with log d_v(P_i, Q)/h_f(P_i) -> L = liminf; L <= 0, so show L >= 0.
Fix m; E(K)/mE(K) is finite, so after passing to a subsequence P_i = [m]P'_i + R with R fixed.
Heights: m^2 h_f(P'_i) = h_f([m]P'_i) + O(1) = h_f(P_i - R) + O(1) <= 2h_f(P_i) + O(1).

If P_i stays v-adically away from Q then L = 0; otherwise P'_i -> Q' with Q = [m]Q' + R after a subsequence, and since P -> [m]P + R is unramified, log d_v(P_i, Q)/log d_v(P'_i, Q') -> 1 (Proposition 2.3).
So L >= lim log d_v(P'_i, Q') / ((1/2) m^2 h_f(P'_i) + O(1)), and Corollary 2.4 gives liminf log d_v(P'_i, Q') / ([K:Q] h_f(P'_i)) >= -2; hence L >= -4[K:Q]/m^2 for every m.
Corollary 3.2.1: an infinite sequence of S-integral points has h_x(P_i) <= #S log|x(P_i)|_v for a fixed v in S along a subsequence, so -log d_v(P_i, O)/h_x(P_i) >= 1/(2#S), contradicting the theorem.

nodes.title: Silverman Corollary IX.3.2.2: for a genus-one curve C/K and nonconstant f, only finitely many P in C(K) have f(P) in R_S
nodes.statement: Let C/K be a curve of genus one over a number field, f in K(C) a nonconstant function and S a finite set of places containing the archimedean ones. Then {P in C(K) : f(P) in R_S} is finite. The statement follows formally from Corollary 3.2.1 after enlarging K and S.

proofSteps: Assume f has a pole at the origin Q of a Weierstrass model y^2 = x^3 + Ax + B, and write f = (phi(x) + psi(x)y)/eta(x).
Pole orders ord_Q(x) = -2, ord_Q(y) = -3, ord_Q(f) < 0 give 2 deg eta < max(2 deg phi, 2 deg psi + 3).
Expanding (f eta(x) - phi(x))^2 = psi(x)^2(x^3 + Ax + B) shows x is integral over K[f]; clear denominators and enlarge S so the leading coefficient is an S-unit.
If f(P) in R_S then x(P) is integral over R_S and lies in K, so x(P) in R_S; apply Corollary 3.2.1.

Check that enlarging S is harmless for finiteness statements.

nodes.title: Silverman Theorem IX.4.1: ax + by = 1 has finitely many solutions in S-units (ineffective proof from Roth), with Evertse's uniform bound quoted
nodes.statement: Let S be a finite set of places of a number field K and a, b in K^*. Then ax + by = 1 has only finitely many solutions x, y in R_S^*. The proof given is ineffective (it uses Roth); Evertse's theorem (quoted without proof) bounds the number of solutions by 3 x 7^{[K:Q] + 2#S} for S containing the archimedean places.
hypotheses: Uses Dirichlet's S-unit theorem (R_S^*/(R_S^*)^m finite) and Roth's theorem
Remark 4.2.2: the proof is ineffective; effective versions use linear forms in logarithms (IX.5, not read)
The printed proof is labelled "INEFFECTIVE PROOF (SKETCH)"; the bound |X/Y - gamma|_v <= C_1/|Y|_v^m is left to Exercise 9.5
proofSteps: Fix m large; write x = c_i X^m, y = c_j Y^m with coset representatives c_i of R_S^*/(R_S^*)^m, reducing to alpha X^m + beta Y^m = 1 with X, Y in R_S.
If there are infinitely many solutions, some v in S has |Y|_v >= H_K(Y)^{1/([K:Q]#S)} for infinitely many.
Factor over m-th roots of unity: prod_zeta (X/Y - zeta gamma) = 1/(alpha Y^m) with gamma^m = -beta/alpha; so X/Y is close to one root and far from the others, |X/Y - gamma|_v <= C_1/|Y|_v^m.
H_K(X/Y) <= C_2 H_K(Y), so |X/Y - gamma|_v <= C H_K(X/Y)^{-m/([K:Q]#S)}.
For m > 2[K:Q]#S Roth gives finitely many X/Y, each giving at most m pairs (X, Y).

nodes.title: Silverman Theorem IX.4.3 and Corollary IX.4.3.1 (Siegel's second proof): y^2 = f(x) with deg f >= 3 and distinct roots has finitely many S-integral solutions
nodes.statement: Let f(x) in K[x] have degree d >= 3 and distinct roots in Kbar. Then y^2 = f(x) has only finitely many solutions x, y in R_S. Consequently (Corollary 4.3.1) for a genus-one curve C/K and nonconstant f in K(C), finitely many P in C(K) have f(P) in R_S. Every step of the reduction to S-unit equations can be made effective, but the finiteness of the S-unit equation used here (Theorem 4.1) is ineffective.
hypotheses: Enlarging K and S: f splits, a in R_S^*, alpha_i - alpha_j in R_S^* for i != j (page image p. 284), and R_S a principal ideal domain
L/K obtained by adjoining square roots of all elements of R_S^* is finite by Dirichlet's S-unit theorem
Corollary 4.3.1 uses the reduction of Corollary 3.2.2 to f = x
proofSteps: A prime of R_S divides at most one x - alpha_i and does not divide a, so each (x - alpha_i)R_S is a square: x - alpha_i = b_i z_i^2 with b_i in R_S^*.
Over L with T the places above S, b_i = beta_i^2, so alpha_j - alpha_i = (beta_i z_i - beta_j z_j)(beta_i z_i + beta_j z_j) with both factors T-units.
Siegel's identity (beta_1 z_1 +- beta_2 z_2)/(beta_1 z_1 - beta_3 z_3) -+ (beta_2 z_2 +- beta_3 z_3)/(beta_1 z_1 - beta_3 z_3) = 1 gives two S-unit equations, so finitely many values of both ratios.
Their product determines (alpha_2 - alpha_1)/(beta_1 z_1 - beta_3 z_3)^2, hence beta_1 z_1 - beta_3 z_3, hence beta_1 z_1, hence x = alpha_1 + (beta_1 z_1)^2, and each x gives at most two y.
acceptance: Check the degree and distinct-root hypotheses: d >= 3 is needed for three roots in Siegel's identity.
State that effectivity would require replacing Theorem 4.1 by an effective S-unit bound (IX.5, not read).

nodes.title: Zhang 1998 Section 1 and Lemma 4.1: torsion subvarieties, Galois orbits, strict, generic and small sequences, and generic subsequences of Zariski-dense sequences
nodes.statement: Let A be an abelian variety over a number field K, sigma : K -> C an embedding, O(x) = Gal(Qbar/K)x the orbit of x in A(Qbar), and h a Neron-Tate height with respect to a symmetric ample line bundle on A. A subvariety Y is torsion if Y = x + B for an abelian subvariety B and a torsion point x. A sequence (x_n) in A(Qbar) is strict if no infinite subsequence lies in a proper torsion subvariety, generic if no infinite subsequence lies in a proper subvariety, and small if h(x_n) -> 0. The orbits O(x_n) are equidistributed with respect to a measure dx on A_sigma(C) if (1/#O(x_n)) sum over y in O(x_n) of f(y) -> integral of f dx for every continuous f. For a variety X over Qbar, every Zariski-dense sequence (x_n) in X has a generic subsequence (Lemma 4.1).

Lemma 4.1 uses that the set of proper subvarieties of X over Qbar is countable
proofSteps: Lemma 4.1: list the proper subvarieties Y_1, Y_2, ... (countably many); for each i pick an element x_{a_i} of the sequence outside Y_1 union ... union Y_i with a_i increasing.
Then (x_{a_i}) meets each Y_j only finitely often, so it is generic.

nodes.title: Zhang 1998 Lemma 3.1 and the stabilizer reduction: for trivial stabilizer G(X), alpha_m : X^m -> A^{m-1} is a generic embedding for m large; in general pass to X/G(X) in A/G(X)
nodes.statement: Let X be an integral subvariety of an abelian variety A over an algebraically closed field with trivial stabilizer G(X) = {a in A : a + X = X}. For m large, alpha_m : X^m -> A^{m-1}, (x_1, ..., x_m) -> (x_1 - x_2, x_2 - x_3, ..., x_{m-1} - x_m), is a generic embedding (quasi-finite with generic degree 1). For general X over a number field, with G = G(X), X' = X/G is a subvariety of A' = A/G, A is isogenous to A' x A'' with A'' the identity component of G, X nontorsion implies X' has positive dimension, and the Bogomolov statement for X in A is equivalent to that for X' in A' (for a symmetric ample line bundle pulled back from A' x A'').

nodes.title: Szpiro-Ullmo-Zhang 1997, Proposition 2.1, Theoreme 3.1, Proposition 4.1 and Theoreme 1.2: generic small sequences equidistribute, and on abelian varieties the limit is Haar measure
nodes.statement: Let X be an arithmetic variety of dimension d over O_K (flat projective with smooth generic fibre) and L a hermitian line bundle with L_K ample, c_1(L_sigma) positive at every archimedean sigma and c1hat(L)^d = 0. If (x_n) in X(Qbar) has h_L(x_n) -> 0 and all subsequences Zariski dense, then for every archimedean sigma and continuous f on X_sigma(C), (1/#O(x_n)) sum over x_n^g in O(x_n) of f(sigma(x_n^g)) -> integral of f d mu with d mu = c_1(L_sigma)^{d-1} / deg. For an abelian variety A over K with symmetric ample L (Proposition 4.1, via Zhang's adelic metrics), the same holds for the Neron-Tate height and d mu is the Haar measure of total mass 1 on A_sigma(C) (Theoreme 1.2). With Raynaud's theorem that strict sequences of torsion points are Zariski dense, strict sequences of torsion points equidistribute (Theoreme 1.1, Corollaire 1.3).

Change the metric at sigma: L(lambda f) with norm multiplied by exp(-lambda f); then h_{L(lambda f)}(x) = h_L(x) + (lambda/#O(x)) sum f(sigma(x^g)), so lim h_{L(lambda f)}(x_i) = lambda C.

Letting lambda -> 0+ gives C >= 0, a contradiction.

Proposition 4.1 repeats the argument with a sequence of models (A_n, L_n) built from [s] : A -> A and the cube metric, using uniform convergence h_{L_n} -> h_L, h_L(A) = 0 and c1hat(L_n)^d -> 0, with errors of size epsilon.

nodes.title: Zhang 1998 Theorem 2.1 with the theorem of successive minima: equidistribution for generic small sequences on possibly singular subvarieties with semipositive adelic metrics
nodes.statement: Let X be a d-dimensional variety over a number field K, L an ample line bundle with a semipositive adelic metric such that h(X) = 0, and sigma an archimedean place. nodes.title: Zhang 1998 Corollary 3 (generalized Bogomolov conjecture): small points of a nontorsion subvariety are not Zariski dense
nodes.statement: Let A be an abelian variety over a number field, h a Neron-Tate height for a symmetric ample line bundle, and X a nontorsion subvariety of A (not a torsion translate of an abelian subvariety). Then there is epsilon > 0 such that {x in X(Qbar) : h(x) <= epsilon} is not Zariski dense in X. For a smooth curve X of genus > 1 embedded in its Jacobian by x -> x - D with deg D = 1, the conjecture was earlier proved when (2g - 2)D - Omega is not torsion and by Ullmo when it is torsion.

The subvariety is integral (Section 3 works with integral X); Corollary 3 is proved in Section 4 under the label "Corollary 1.2", which does not exist in the printed paper (cross-reference slip)
Uses the asserted reduction to trivial stabilizer, Lemma 3.1, Lemma 4.1, the theorem of successive minima and Theorem 2.1 on both X^m and alpha_m(X^m)
The measure comparison dx_m = alpha_m^*(dx'_m) is stated as "It follows that", from the two equidistribution limits and generic injectivity of alpha_m at the points x(n_i)

Suppose (x_n) is a Zariski-dense small sequence on X. For any m and a bijection N -> N^m, the induced sequence x(n) on X^m is Zariski dense and has a generic subsequence x(n_i) (Lemma 4.1).
Take m large so alpha_m is a generic embedding (Lemma 3.1), and pass to a subsequence where alpha_m is smooth at x(n_i).
Give X^m and A^{m-1} the product admissible metrics; x(n_i) and alpha_m(x(n_i)) are small, and by successive minima both X^m and alpha_m(X^m) have height 0.
Theorem 2.1 on X^m: delta_{x(n_i)} -> dx_m = p_1^*(dx) ... p_m^*(dx). On alpha_m(X^m): delta_{alpha_m(x(n_i))} -> dx'_m, the restriction of (sum pi_i^* c_1(L_A))^{m dim X} / deg.

Hence dx_m = alpha_m^*(dx'_m). At a smooth point x of X_sigma(C), dx_m is nonzero at (x, ..., x), while alpha_m contracts the diagonal to 0 and is singular there, so alpha_m^* dx'_m vanishes: contradiction.
acceptance: This is the Bogomolov branch required by RP.5: relative to a symmetric ample line bundle, a geometrically irreducible nontorsion subvariety has a positive height threshold below which points are not Zariski dense.

nodes.statement: Let X_K be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve of genus g >= 2 over a number field K, J its Jacobian, D_0 a divisor of degree 1 and phi_{D_0} : X_K -> J the associated embedding. (Theoreme 1.1) There is epsilon > 0 such that {P in X_K(Kbar) : h_NT(phi_{D_0}(P)) <= epsilon} is finite. (Theoreme 1.2) If the minimal regular model X of X_K has semistable reduction, then (omega_Ar, omega_Ar)_Ar >= (omega_a, omega_a)_a > 0.
hypotheses: Zhang's admissible pairing (Invent. Math. 112, 1993) supplies: Theoreme 1.1 when (omega_a, omega_a)_a > 0 and when [Omega - (2g - 2)D_0] is not torsion; failure of Theoreme 1.1 when (omega_a, omega_a)_a = 0 and D_0 = Omega/(2g - 2); Lemme 2.1 (approximation of h_{omega_a} by Arakelov heights over extensions K_n); Lemme 2.2 (h_NT(j(P)) = g/(2g - 2) h_{omega_a}(P)). These are imports; the paper is in the supplied library but was not read
Theoreme 2.3 is the Szpiro-Ullmo-Zhang equidistribution theorem for abelian varieties; Theoreme 2.4 is an extension of their Theoreme 3.1 to a sequence of models, proved in the paper
Fibres of s : X^g -> J, s(P_1, ..., P_g) = j(P_1) + ... + j(P_g), are linear systems (Milne, Jacobian varieties, Chapter 5, not read); s is generically finite of degree g!
The proof is independent of Raynaud's theorem on torsion points, which Theoreme 1.1 generalizes
proofSteps: Assume (omega_a, omega_a)_a = 0 and D_0 = Omega/(2g - 2) is K-rational; Zhang gives a generic sequence t_k in X_K(Kbar) with h_{omega_a}(t_k) -> 0.

Theoreme 2.4 with Lemme 2.1: the Galois orbits of t_k are dense in X(C); build y_n = (x_{n,1}, ..., x_{n,g}) in X^g inductively, with h_{omega_a}(x_{n,i}) -> 0, orbits 1/n-dense, and dim H^0(O(x_{n,1} + ... + x_{n,g})) = 1 (Proposition 3.1, Lemme 3.2).
Then y_n is generic in X^g, z_n = s(y_n) is generic and small in J, and s is a bijection from O(y_n) onto O(z_n).
Lemme 4.1: Theoreme 2.4 for the product metric gives equidistribution of O(y_n) to pi_1^* nu ^ ... ^ pi_g^* nu. Lemme 4.2: Theoreme 2.3 gives equidistribution of O(z_n) to Haar measure mu_H.
Lemmes 4.3-4.4: comparing the two limits through the orbit bijection gives s^* d mu_H = g! pi_1^* nu ^ ... ^ pi_g^* nu.

Contradiction: writing mu_H via translation-invariant forms, s^* d mu_H vanishes at points (P_1, ..., P_g) with h^0(Omega(-P_1 - ... - P_g)) > 0 (e.g. (P_0, ..., P_0) for a Weierstrass point P_0), while the product of the nu is everywhere strictly positive.

nodes.title: Frontier register: Bombieri-Lang and Lang, finiteness of Shafarevich-Tate groups, BSD rank, sufficiency of obstructions, and Lang-type height and rank conjectures, with what is proved
nodes.statement: The following are conjectural and must not be consumed as proved. (1) Bombieri-Lang (Poonen Conjecture 9.5.11): for a geometrically integral positive-dimensional variety X of general type over a number field k, X(k) is not Zariski dense. (2) Lang (Poonen Conjecture 9.5.12): such X has a proper closed S with (X - S)(L) finite for all finite L/k. Both are proved for subvarieties of abelian varieties (Faltings [Fal91], cited). (3) Shafarevich-Tate (Poonen Conjecture 5.7.32; Silverman Conjecture X.4.13): Sha(A) is finite; known for elliptic curves over Q only when the analytic rank is at most 1. (4) BSD rank part (Poonen Conjecture 5.7.33): ord_{s=1} L(A, s) = rk A(k); known for elliptic curves over Q of analytic rank at most 1. (5) Sufficiency of obstructions: "the Brauer-Manin obstruction is the only one" (Definition 8.2.8) is a property of a class of varieties and fails in general (Theorems 8.6.1, 8.6.5); for smooth complete intersections of dimension >= 3 the descent and Brauer-Manin sets are all of X(A) (Theorem 8.6.12, sketch), so neither obstruction can detect a failure of the local-global principle, and no smooth hypersurface of dimension >= 3 is known to fail it. (6) Lang-type conjectures in Silverman: arbitrarily large ranks (VIII.10.1), lower bounds for hhat in terms of the discriminant (VIII.9.9), bounds on generators (VIII.10.2) and on the number of integral points (IX.3.5).

nodes.statement: Let K be a function field with field of constants k (k algebraically closed in K = k(V)), and X a regular projective geometrically integral K-curve of genus > 1 with X(K) infinite. If char k = 0 then X is constant (X = Y_K); if char k = p then X is isotrivial (constant after a finite extension); moreover X is nice. nodes.statement: Let X be a nice k-curve of genus g with a k-point. There is a g-dimensional abelian variety J = Jac X with J(L) isomorphic to Pic^0(X_L) functorially in field extensions L/k, and J(T) = {L in Pic(X x T) : deg L_t = 0 for all t} / pi^* Pic T for k-schemes T. The Picard scheme Pic_{X/k} has components Pic^n, with Pic^0 = J and 0 -> J -> Pic_{X/k} -> Z -> 0.

gaps.title: Mordell-Weil for abelian varieties: the height part, and descent when n meets the residue characteristic, are not read
gaps.detail: Poonen Theorem 5.7.31 proves the weak Mordell-Weil theorem through Selmer sets (Theorem 8.4.9). For the height part it only says "Combining this with the theory of height functions completes the proof; see [Ser97, 4.3]". Serre, Lectures on the Mordell-Weil theorem, was not read. Theorem 8.4.9 assumes that char k does not divide m. Poonen also asserts without proof that the coboundary and the evaluation map A(k) -> H^1(k, A[m]) coincide. Next source action: read Serre, Lectures on the Mordell-Weil theorem, Chapters 3-4, and Milne, Arithmetic Duality Theorems, III for flat cohomology.
